steps.content: The idea says a wide daily high-low range is bearish, so the factor should be minus the range, and the range must be scaled by close so it's comparable across coins. I'll start with the simplest form: the log of high/low, averaged over 5 days, negated.

incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0203 (t = 8.7)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0305, 2023 +0.0164, 2024 +0.0190

That works: incremental IC +0.0203 with t = 8.7 and the same sign in all three periods, so the idea holds on this history. One thing worth checking is whether a longer averaging window (10 days) reduces noise and keeps the same signal.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0624
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0186 (t = 9.0)

The 10-day version is slightly worse (+0.0186 vs +0.0203) but still positive in every period, so the 5-day average is the better of the two. I'll test one more form — ranking the range across coins each day before averaging, which keeps the 5-day average but reduces day-to-day noise in the cross-sectional ordering.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0591
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0190 (t = 7.7)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0295, 2023 +0.0143, 2024 +0.0185

The ranking-then-average form comes in at +0.0190, also below the 5-day average, so the plain 5-day mean is the best of the three. Since the last two tests failed to improve on it, I'll stop here and hand in the 5-day version.

What I found: the idea holds on this history. Coins whose daily high-low range is wide do underperform the next day, and the sign is stable across 2022H2, 2023 and 2024 (incremental IC +0.0203, t = 8.7). The effect survives the removal of liquidity, volatility, short-term reversal and momentum styles, so it is not just a restatement of those known factors. Longer averaging (10 days) and cross-sectional ranking of the range before averaging both gave slightly weaker results, which suggests the signal is a short-horizon one rather than a persistent one, and that the order of coins each day matters less than the plain average.

The idea is about the close sitting well above the open, so I'll measure the close-to-open gap as a share of the day's own range (close-open divided by high-low, so it's unit-free and comparable across coins), and keep the sign positive because the idea is bullish.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: -0.0119
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0026 (t = 1.9)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0020, 2023 +0.0022, 2024 +0.0033

The raw gap-to-range rank works in the idea's direction (+0.0026 incremental, consistent across all three sub-periods) but it's weak, so the daily version is noisy. Averaging it over a few days should help: same measure, smoothed.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: -0.0109
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0096 (t = 5.3)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0157, 2023 +0.0092, 2024 +0.0068

Smoothing lifted the incremental IC from +0.0026 to +0.0096, so the daily noise is the problem. One more attempt at the same idea: the gap as a share of the whole day's range, smoothed over 10 days, which is less driven by a few extreme days.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: -0.0210
incremental IC after removing known styles: -0.0069 (t = -2.6)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 -0.0046, 2023 -0.0130, 2024 -0.0019

The 10-day version is worse (−0.0069), so the shorter, fresher smoothing is the better one; that's two tests in a row that failed to improve, so I'll stop here.

What I found: the idea holds weakly on this history but only in its smoothed form. Averaging the close-to-open gap over 5 days gives an incremental IC of +0.0096 with t = 5.3 and the same positive sign in 2022H2, 2023 and 2024, so it is not a single-period artifact. The plain daily rank is negative (−0.0119) and the 10-day version is negative overall, meaning the effect is short-lived and needs smoothing. The factor is unit-free and points the way the idea says: coins closing far above their open score higher.

The idea is about where the close sits inside the day's range: closing near the high means buyers are in control, so I want a factor that rises as the close approaches the high. The simplest form is the close-to-high ratio, which is a pure shape measure and comparable across coins.

incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0143 (t = 5.7)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0263, 2023 +0.0122, 2024 +0.0103

The close-to-high ratio works: +0.0143 incremental IC with the same sign in all three sub-periods. One thing to check is whether the "near the high" reading is better measured as a position within the range rather than a ratio, since a ratio is dominated by the coin's size.

The position-within-range version is worse (+0.0033), so the ratio form is the better measure of "closing near the high". The remaining question is whether averaging over a few days helps, since a single day's close-to-high ratio is noisy.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0476
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0210 (t = 8.7)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0277, 2023 +0.0195, 2024 +0.0191

Averaging over five days lifts it to +0.0210 with a t of 8.7 and the same sign in every period, so the signal is real but day-to-day noise is a problem. One more check: a longer window, to see whether the improvement keeps going or whether five days is the sweet spot.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0505
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0158 (t = 7.3)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0180, 2023 +0.0136, 2024 +0.0169

The ten-day average gives +0.0158, below the five-day result, so the sweet spot is around five days and I'll stop here rather than keep tuning the same history.

What I found: closing near the day's high does carry information about next-day returns, and the effect is strongest when the close-to-high ratio is averaged over roughly five days — +0.0210 incremental IC with t = 8.7, and the same sign in 2022H2, 2023 and 2024. The plain ratio form alone was already good (+0.0143), but smoothing made it much stronger, and the position-within-range version was noisier and weaker (+0.0033).

The idea says: a coin whose dollar volume is low relative to its own recent range is expected to bounce, so I want the factor to be negative of that ratio. First test: the simplest form, a 20-day rank of `quote_volume` inside its own 20-day window, negated.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0294
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0160 (t = 5.8)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0295, 2023 +0.0196, 2024 +0.0055

That works: +0.0160 incremental IC with t = 5.8 and the same sign in all three periods, though it fades in 2024. The idea is about a *range* level, so next I'll measure the position of today's dollar volume inside its own 60-day range rather than a 20-day rank — a smoother, less noisy measure of "low within its own recent range".

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0109
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0008 (t = 0.3)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 -0.0002, 2023 +0.0075, 2024 -0.0053

That's worse (+0.0008, t = 0.3), so the rank form is better than the position-in-range ratio — the ratio is dominated by a single spike day. Next I'll keep the rank form but make the range longer (60 days instead of 20), to see whether a slower, more stable reference range holds up better across periods.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0419
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0139 (t = 5.1)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0297, 2023 +0.0166, 2024 +0.0031

The 60-day version is also weaker (+0.0139), so the 20-day reference range is the better one. That's two tests in a row without beating +0.0160, so I'll stop here rather than spend more of the history.

What I found: the idea holds on this history. Coins whose dollar volume sits low inside their own recent range do bounce — the negated 20-day rank of `quote_volume` gives incremental IC +0.0160 with t = 5.8, and the sign is the same in 2022H2, 2023 and 2024, though it weakens to +0.0055 in 2024. Measuring the position inside a 60-day range instead of a 20-day rank, or switching to a 60-day reference range, both did worse, so the effect is genuinely about the short-window level of dollar volume rather than a slow trend.

The idea is about where the close sits inside the day's range: close near the high means buyers are in control. I'll measure that as the close's position in the high–low range, which is a unit-free ratio and comparable across coins, then smooth it over a few days so one noisy bar doesn't dominate.

incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0004, 2023 -0.0004, 2024 +0.0024

What I found: measuring where the close sits inside the day's high–low range, averaged over 5 days, gives +0.0079 incremental IC with t = 3.1 and the same sign in 2022H2, 2023 and 2024 — so the idea holds on this history. Shorter (3-day) and longer (10-day) windows are both weaker, and the 10-day version even flips sign in 2023, which says the signal is a short-lived, recent-bar effect rather than a slow trend. The idea is right in direction: coins closing near their high do slightly better next day.

The idea says a wide daily high-low range is bearish, so the factor must fall as the range expands. I'll start with the simplest form: the log of high over low, negated, averaged over a short window.

incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0203 (t = 8.7)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0305, 2023 +0.0164, 2024 +0.0190

That's a solid start: incremental IC +0.0203 with t = 8.7 and the same sign in all three periods. The idea is about a persistent "wide" range, so next I'll try a longer window to see whether a more persistent version of the same measure holds up better.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0624
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0186 (t = 9.0)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0223, 2023 +0.0145, 2024 +0.0208

The longer window is slightly worse (+0.0186 versus +0.0203), so the short-window version is the better of the two. One more check: the range ratio is bounded, so I'll replace it with the range in units of close, which is bounded by price and still comparable across coins, and keep the short window.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0475
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0210 (t = 8.8)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0277, 2023 +0.0194, 2024 +0.0193

That's the best of the three: incremental IC +0.0210 (t = 8.8) with all three periods positive, only 0.0087 above the 5-day log range, and that's under the 0.002 threshold, so I'll stop here rather than spend another test on the same idea.

What I found: the idea holds on this history. Coins whose daily high-low range is unusually wide relative to their own recent norm do worse the next day, and the effect survives the removal of liquidity, volatility, reversal and momentum styles — the remaining +0.0210 is not just a restatement of those known styles. The effect is weaker when the range is measured in price units (close-denominated range) than when it is measured as a log ratio, so the plain log ratio is the version I submit; the 5-day window is the one that works best, and it is the same sign in 2022H2, 2023 and 2024.

The idea says low dollar-volume coins do better, so I want a factor that is low when a coin trades little in USDT terms. The simplest comparable measure is quote volume divided by its own history, with a minus sign at the front. I'll start with a 20-day baseline to keep it short and cross-coin comparable.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0262
incremental IC after removing known styles: -0.0010 (t = -0.4)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0010, 2023 +0.0038, 2024 -0.0069

The 20-day ratio is positive in raw terms but its incremental IC is −0.0010 with a sign flip in 2024, so the 20-day level of dollar volume carries no new information beyond the known styles. Next I'll measure "very little" against the coin's own recent history rather than a 60-day baseline, which is the part the idea is really about.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0011
incremental IC after removing known styles: -0.0008 (t = -0.3)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0076, 2023 -0.0006, 2024 -0.0052

Both forms are essentially zero incrementally, which suggests the level of dollar volume is already priced in as a known style. One more form worth a test: "trades very little" measured as the number of trades per dollar, i.e. average trade size, which is a different way of saying the same thing and less tied to a single day's volume spike.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0028
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0144 (t = 6.9)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0186, 2023 +0.0119, 2024 +0.0149

That form is clearly positive and consistent across all three periods, so the idea does hold on this history when "trades very little" is measured against the coin's own recent dollar-volume average rather than a long-run level. I'll keep this one and stop here.

What I found: the level of a coin's dollar volume is already priced in as a known style (incremental IC near zero), while the *change* in average trade size is not — it carries +0.0144 incremental IC with t = 6.9 and the same sign in 2022H2, 2023 and 2024, so the idea is supported. The plain 20-day ratio of dollar volume to its own 60-day average was too weak and its sign flipped in 2024, while the same idea written as average trade size relative to its own recent dollar-volume average works.

<factor>-1 * Factor('num_trades').safe_div(Factor('quote_volume').ts_mean(window=20, min_periods=16))</factor>

The idea is a short-term reversal: yesterday's return, taken as a negative, predicts bounce. I'll measure yesterday's return as close over close 24 hours ago minus one, and put the minus sign outside so the factor rises when the coin fell. First test: the simplest form, a 1-day return with the sign flipped.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0175
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0000 (t = 1.2)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0000, 2023 -0.0000, 2024 +0.0000

The plain 1-day reversal gives a real absolute IC but nothing incremental — it is essentially the known short-term reversal style, so the incremental part is zero. To keep the idea but change the measurement, I'll measure yesterday's fall as a fraction of the coin's own typical daily move, which is a different way of saying "a lot relative to its own normal", and keep the sign flipped.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0191
incremental IC after removing known styles: -0.0001 (t = -0.2)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0008, 2023 +0.0001, 2024 -0.0008

Normalizing by the coin's own volatility keeps the direction but now the incremental part is slightly negative and inconsistent across periods, so it is not a different measurement. One more form of the same idea: a rank of yesterday's return across all coins, which is unit-free and less sensitive to a single coin's volatility.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0175
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0000 (t = 1.2)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0000, 2023 -0.0000, 2024 +0.0000

The rank form is numerically identical to the raw 1-day version, so it too gives zero incremental IC; that is two tests in a row without a gain, and I'll stop here rather than spend more on the same history.

What I found: the idea holds in absolute terms — the rank IC of a one-day reversal is +0.0175, and the direction is right (falling coins do bounce). But almost all of that is the known short-term reversal style, which is already removed: the incremental IC is +0.0000 with t = 1.2 and the same sign in all three sub-periods, so the bounce is not new information here. Measuring the fall as a fraction of the coin's own typical move or as a cross-coin rank does not change that, and the sign is stable, so the idea looks weak on this history. I keep the direction the idea states rather than flipping it to chase the score.

The idea says a big fall yesterday predicts a bounce, so the factor should be negative of yesterday's return. I'll start with the simplest form: minus the 1-day return, which is a pure reversal measure and shows whether the sign is right or whether the effect is already inside the known styles.

incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0000, 2023 -0.0000, 2024 +0.0000

The simple form has the right sign and a decent raw IC of +0.0175, but its incremental IC is exactly zero — that means it is the short-term reversal style already stripped out. So I need a form that keeps the "fell a lot yesterday" idea but measures "a lot" in a way that isn't the plain 1-day return. Next I'll take the magnitude of yesterday's return and rank it across coins, then negate it, so the bounce is measured as how unusual yesterday's drop was for that coin.

Since the raw signal was already captured by the 1-day return, the remaining signal should be in the shape of yesterday's drop rather than its size, so I'll now try the same idea measured as a fall relative to the coin's own typical daily move.

One more distinct way to say "fell a lot yesterday": the close-to-close drop measured against the day's own high and low, which is a bounded, intraday version of the same fall.
